should be taken out of the hands of the military and placed in the hands of the civil authorities.
I am afraid we cannot agree with that point of view. There are negotiations taking place for a truce. In the very nature of -things, they are matters of a purely military nature, and should remain with the forces in the field, acting on instructions from their own governments, until agreement is reached. That has been the well accepted course followed down through the years, and I do not think there -should be any departure from it today.
As a matter of fact we are now in one of those periods of recurring optimism with respect to the truce talks, and any drastic change in the structure of the present negotiations might hinder rather than help a speedy settlement.
The leader of the C.C.F. went further and indicated that the time was ripe, not only to pursue the course mentioned but also to accord diplomatic recognition to red China. In my opinion, to give such recognition to a *declared aggressor would be to reward aggression itself. It should not be done at this stage. It will be time enough to consider diplomatic recognition, the taking into membership in the United Nations and a number of Far Eastern issues when communist China gives evidence to the world that she has abandoned her program of aggression and has entered into a satisfactory peace settlement which will guarantee stability to the Far East.
I should like to point out if I may something I said in the debate on February 5, 1951, with respect to our position concerning red China. My speech was made just after I came from -the meetings of the United Nations general assembly in New York. I have no intention of reading into the record more than one paragraph, but I think this is closely allied to some of the matters which I have been discussing. I quote from page 75 of Hansard of February 5, 1951, as follows:
Canadians will hope fervently that the free world will continue to leave no stone unturned to bring the Orient and the Occident into peaceful and harmonious relationships. The door to further negotiation must still be left open for an honourable and just settlement. If I were to underline any part of the speech I am making this afternoon, it would be those two sentences. We do not want a war with Asia; we do not want a war with anyone. We want to help Asia. But naturally we want to be certain that we are not assisting in the building of a giant Soviet empire designed to overthrow us and the rest of the world when we are offering the hand of genuine help to peoples who sorely need it. So we say to the red Chinese government: Get rid of your Muscovite masters, and be your own. We can deal with Chinese as Chinese, but their membership in the imperial

Soviet family puts unnecessarily high hurdles in front of free democratic assistance. Take those hurdles down and let us work together in peace, harmony and understanding. We all have much to contribute together, but less to contribute alone.
I come now to another point, a Pacific pact which was a matter mentioned by the minister of external affairs this afternoon, although he did not enlarge upon government policy with respect to it. It may be that that policy is static, that it remains the same as it was previously. It seems to me that our foreign policy, looking toward protection by strength of our free way of life, should not neglect the Pacific area in any plans that are made. The red planners for world domination appear to heed the language of power and might above everything else. Nothing seems to encourage them more than evidence of hesitancy or uncertainty in the policies of others. It was the failure of the free world- to make plain their feelings to these diabolical planners in June, 1950, that played a big part in their decision to cross the 38th parallel in Korea. The Far East of today, as well -as other areas of the free world, could be placed in jeopardy through a division of views on free-power policies.
We must not take the chance of having another Korea. This party has previously called for the consideration of a Pacific pact. It believes that as time moves on the argument in its favour becomes more convincing than ever. The implementation of such a policy would give a measure of stability in the Far East and would enable us to proceed with our plans for the rehabilitation of those areas in the Asiatic free world which are so essential to peace itself.
There are further problems which arise and we must make it abundantly clear that we are ready to deal with them as well. I should like to refer to another part of the Far East. When people discuss in a loose and sometimes critical way the contribution which the British commonwealth can make to world peace, they quite often seem to overlook one part of that commonwealth which perhaps can make the greatest contribution toward better relations and stability as between the east and the west. Something like four out of five people in the British commonwealth of nations are Asiatics. That means that the commonwealth becomes an effective and practical link between the free powers of the western world and the free powers of the Orient. In my opinion part of the keystone in the arch of our efforts to save democracy in the generations to come is that link provided by the commonwealth between Canada, the United Kingdom, India, Pakistan and Ceylon.

Anyone who overlooks the vast possibilities of bringing the east and west together under the aegis of the commonwealth is overlooking something which is practical and which should always be uppermost in our mind. Along with other hon. members, I was interested in the Indian elections which resulted in a great victory for Prime Minister Nehru. One feature of that election which was of some concern to the western world was the large communist vote polled in certain sections of southern India, particularly in the provinces of Travancore and Cochin. I understand from those who come from India that the reason for the communist vote being heavier in those provinces than in some other places was that there was an unsatisfactory type of provincial government there. This indicates not only that, communism can be a positive thing in certain places but that it can be a vehicle for a negative expression against existing institutions, existing forms of government and existing political parties.
One lesson that should be taken from these Indian elections is that we in this country and in the commonwealth must see to it that we use every means at our command to see that the free democratic parties of India, Pakistan and Ceylon are given every help possible so that they remain the governments of those countries in the days that lie ahead and so that communism will not have a chance to take control. I regard India, or perhaps I should say the subcontinent of India, as being the bulwark and bastion of democracy for the next twenty-five or fifty years in the Far East. They will have a great opportunity to provide leadership for that part of the world which is moving toward independence and shaking off from their necks the yoke of domination. I think we can be mighty proud of the Indian, Pakistani and Ceylonese people for the stand they have taken and the way they have held out. At a time when less courageous people and those with less vision would not have held out, they have provided us with at least a first-class bridgehead for democracy where, during this period, we otherwise might not have had a bridgehead at all.
So I think when we are considering the question of our contribution to the Colombo plan we should have these things in mind. I was very interested last Monday night to hear the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), in a brilliant exposition over the air with a number of press representatives, stress one of his favorite themes, that we ought to increase our contribution to the Colombo plan. Our estimated expenditure for
External Affairs
next year is $4,300 million, half of which is to be devoted to the effort to save democracy and the peace. Of that $2,100 million only $25 million is to be used in an attempt to salvage and help India, which occupies a key position in the world today. I believe the government should carefully consider the allocation of money for various expenditures, because in some respects it would seem that we are doing our utmost to close the door on one side of the world while leaving it ajar on another. Not much would be required. It would not be a matter of interfering with our military preparedness program in respect to NATO. I have no doubt that if the minister were to go through the various departments and comb out all unnecessary expenditures, we could give another $25 million to India without scarcely requiring even another vote by parliament. I think we must face that situation, because if India gets on her feet democracy will prevail in the Orient. If India does not get on her feet, then of course we and they are in peril.
Now for a moment I want to return to our obligations with respect to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I for one believe we should do everything we can to achieve a united Canada as far as the prosecution of our plans for world peace is concerned. There is enough division in the world now without our contributing further to it. In that connection I think the government must bear its full share of responsibility for the promotion and continuance of a united program. It is all very well for the minister and the government to say they are watching vigilantly to see how many people on this side of the house are going to support them in their Far Eastern policies and so on. Why, you would think he was trying to catch some of the people off guard on some of these academic questions. Instead of that, if I may say so, the minister should be recognizing his own responsibility for the confusion that exists in the public mind right across Canada.
I was very interested in what the minister said today. To tell the truth I felt rather sympathetic toward him when the hon. member for Lake Centre asked who was responsible for that bad NATO press report. It took the minister a while to get around to it, but he finally said, "Yes, I am the bad boy." He did not use those words, but I imagine everyone knew what he meant. When you have been in diplomacy all your life it must be easy to use language some of the rest of us do not always understand. There has been far too much loose and unconnected talk, if I may say, about NATO goals, NATO plans, NATO blueprints, NATO targets, and NATO hopes. No doubt some of these things have to be done in the

External Affairs
ordinary course of events, but my great complaint is that not enough emphasis has been laid upon giving the public of the free world the bold, clear and understandable truth. It is one thing to throw a lot of big, fancy words on the pages of Hansard; it is another to understand them. Today the minister almost apologized for his use of the word "infrastructure", which I thought meant a kind of undercarriage but which he says has something to do with collective facilities. The public rebels against that kind of description of what NATO is doing. If the North Atlantic governments want to ensure a powerful and united public opinion behind them in their policies, they can best achieve that by telling the people in ordinary terms what is going on and what is proposed to be done.
That is all we are asking. I do not think you will get unity of purpose across the country unless the government takes the lead and does its share. Everyone in this house, no matter to what party he belongs, has as much interest in seeing that we keep out of war and that peace comes in our time as the minister or any of the other top brass in the cabinet. No one has a monopoly on that. We may not be quite as well informed, because after all we have not the battalions of technical people behind us that they have; but that is no reason why we should not pound this government to find out what is going on. And that is exactly what we are trying to do.
Accepting the view that communist imperialism may or may not necessarily march next week but that it nevertheless constitutes a positive threat to our security, the question arises as to how we can best meet the problems caused by a protracted period of cold war. A solution of that problem will come much more easily if the government will tell this house, and through it the Canadian people, the full extent of cabinet commitments made on behalf of the Canadian people to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I know it will be said that some of these details must be kept secret, that it is not in the interest of NATO generally to disclose them. Well, when the last war was on I seem to recall that similar words were uttered. There were governmental objections from time to time on that very basis, but in the end parliamentary pressure was able to compel the disclosure of at least many of the essential details so the public could gain a fuller understanding of what the nation faced and the reasons underlying the heavy taxation. If that could be done in war-and it was done partially anyway-surely there is no reason why it should not be done in peace. I do not need to tell the government there is confusion in the public mind over fMr. Graydon. ]
these matters; they are quite well aware of that fact themselves. That is plain from the approach of the minister of external affairs, his tone of voice and his anxiety to see that this confusion is removed. My own feeling is that without in any way jeopardizing the position of NATO with respect to security or secrecy, parliament should be made aware of the following essential facts:
1.	What have Canadians been asked to contribute to the North Atlantic peace pool in terms of military assistance, processed materials for defence, money, raw materials and other forms of help: (a) before the Lisbon meeting and (b) at the Lisbon meeting?
2.	Of these, what have we undertaken to provide?
3.	What plans has this government instituted to discharge these undertakings?
Parliament should be assured also that all waste will be eliminated, if we are to build up a high public morale and enthusiasm and resolution and determination to see this NATO thing through.
Do not make any mistake about that, Mr. Speaker. The public are going to ask this government not to spend one extra five-cent piece by way of extravagance and waste in the process. I think that has an important bearing on the whole problem of public relations and public morale which is so necessary at this time. I feel that parliament should be assured that waste and extravagance in defence and non-defence expenditures will be eliminated, and that the practice of overstating progress in rearmament, which tends to create a sense of false security, will be discontinued. After all this afternoon the minister admitted issuing this statement from Lisbon which had so many booming and buoyant characteristics about it. No doubt he had learned that lesson from this government; that has been their tendency. I want to say that that ought to be discontinued, whether it is here, whether it is in NATO or wherever it may be. Really no progress will be made by overstating the case. What the people want to know are the clear understandable facts stated in language that ordinary people like ourselves understand.
When I last spoke on this subject in this house I made a proposal to the minister which he more or less shrugged off. I suppose he was thinking about the Far East at that time. In any event, he shrugged off my suggestion about a national development and production board. I went into detail with respect to that before, and I am not going into detail about it this afternoon. I do feel that a national development and production

board, set up in co-operation with the provinces tor the purpose of making a survey of our natural resources, would be useful. Such a board should contain some of the best brains in the country in agriculture, industry, business, labour and the important professions as well as other sections of our national life. It would be of some help to Canada today in preparing to meet its commitments to NATO. It would be an important step in connection with the development of our mineral and other strategic resources, and a means of enhancing our capacity to shoulder many of our obligations under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I have examined this proposal with a good deal of care and consideration, and I put it forward with all the earnestness that I can summon. I hope that the government will see in it some measure of benefit and advantage to this nation in these critical times.
I am the first to admit that the problem facing this administration, and indeed every other government participating in NATO, of keeping at high enthusiastic levels the national resolution and determination to see this thing through, is a gigantic one. It will not be done merely by a government saying it has to be done. It will be done by the masses of our people, with a full realization of the magnitude of the threat to our security and in possession of the information as to how comprehensive is our part in the combined pool and as to what steps are required at home to carry it out. There is no point in deceiving ourselves that the superimposition of a program of defence preparedness on top of a normal peacetime economy, without the mass psychology of war to support it, is going to be any easy policy to carry out.
I do not propose to make the task of this government any more difficult than it is by anything that I shall say or do. I do say to the government in conclusion that my main reason in asking them to take fully into their confidence the people who man our defences and pay the shot is in order to present to the world a united Canadian team for peace.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on one remark made at the very outset of the minister's speech. He said he hoped that, in principle, all parties would stand together on international affairs. If the principle he had in mind is that Canada should resist both communist aggression and a revival of fascism or nazism throughout the world, we accept that principle, and I hope other members of the house do also. We believe that wherever human freedom is threatened, those of us who believe in individual liberty and
External Affairs
democratic institutions must stand together. But in carrying into effect that principle we believe that there are other than military means which must be taken into account; in other words, that the raising of the standard of living, the feeding of the hungry, amongst the depressed peoples everywhere is the best insurance in the long run that we shall have against both communism and nazism or any other form of totalitarianism.
One result of the criticisms that we have made of the Lisbon conference statement has been the achievement of considerable clarification of the NATO objectives agreed to by the Atlantic nations at the recent conference. After all, Mr. Speaker, I have always believed that the functions of an opposition should be to criticize the statements of the government, and to endeavour to get at the real facts in any situation with which we are faced. As a matter of fact, there are some matters which are not yet clarified, even after the minister's speech of March 13 when he gave information of a type very much like that which he has given us this afternoon, and when he took responsibility to some extent for the Lisbon press conference statement and admitted that it was ambiguous. The Toronto Globe and Mail of last Saturday went further than that and said:
Ambiguous is hardly the word for the communique and the summary. If Mr. Pearson is correct, these documents were a pack of nonsense, not to say a pack of lies.
That is pretty strong language. I would not go that far myself, although I was very critical of the minister about the statement that was issued at Lisbon. I think it was a statement that was wrapped up in such language that it was deliberately designed to mislead the people, particularly those on the North American continent. The London Times, the London Economist and other papers with an international reputation considered that there had been a vast increase in the targets. They had been discussing, as we all had been discussing, 25 or 30 divisions in 1952 and 60 divisions in 1954, as the target which the NATO countries had in mind. Those goals, may I add, did seem both attainable and reasonable. Then the communique seemed to indicate there would be an increase and that view, let me add, was reinforced by an address that many of us heard over the air by the United States secretary of state for foreign affairs, Mr. Acheson, on February 29 when he said there had been an increase, and that was taken at its face value. I want to say to the minister that up to now I believe there has been a great deal of confusion and that, in any event, I think that the chairman of the conference-in this case the minister-and his colleagues are to be criticized because,

External Affairs
knowing that this confusion existed, they were so tardy in removing the cause of it. Unless the matter had been brought forward in a striking manner not only here but in several other places, no clarification might have been made for a considerable time. It is apparent that for a whole year the real goals or targets were higher than we in this parliament and elsewhere were led to believe. I say that when a condition of this sort is exposed it has a bad effect, because it undermines confidence in such organizations and the statements which they issue from time to time.
Of course, if this was done last year in the interests of secrecy, I submit that it was bound to fail in its objective because, I think, probably from our own published reports, our own statements made in this parliament and those made in other parliaments of the Atlantic nations the Soviet union understands perfectly well what our rearmament program is, what our manpower situation is, and what the economic circumstances of all the NATO nations really are. I therefore say that it could not fulfil the objective if that was the objective that was in mind during the last year. I am also certain that if the information had been given at the time, that information might have been understood. But because the targets were large I think that there was a fear on the part of the Atlantic nations that some of the countries at least might be filled with consternation. I am equally sure that had these military targets that evidently were in contemplation a year ago been revealed, there would have been more insistence upon the part of many of us-and I include myself in this group-on the giving of more economic aid to the nations in order that they might bear the burden being imposed upon them.
Apart from matters that must of necessity, in circumstances of this sort, remain secret lest there be given to the enemy information which the enemy should not have, I say to the minister that democratic peoples have the right to know all the facts; that is, as I say, without jeopardizing the security that we must carefully guard.
The minister said again this afternoon that he did not know where the idea came from that a budget of some $300 billion had been adopted at the NATO conference by the NATO nations; that is, $300 billion for the next three years. As a matter of fact, that information was headlined in all the Canadian papers. It was carried in the great papers across the world. Indeed, we were told that this budget had been adopted unanimously at the Lisbon conference.

No; but I say that all the newspapers reporting the conference told us that was so. As a matter of fact, failing any other authoritative statement from the Lisbon conference, we naturally accepted that as being the true state of affairs. I must say at once that when you look at the budgets of the nations already for their military equipment and so on over the next three years, as has been outlined from time to time, you can understand why it was that there was considerable criticism and indeed a great deal of misgiving in the minds of most of the people who read those stories from Lisbon. The United States' budget for armaments is $171 billion over the next three years, as far as we are able to find out from reliable sources.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For all defence, including the Far East.

Yes, that is for all defence, including NATO defence. The defence budget of the United Kingdom for all purposes is about $13 billion; that of France about $12 billion; our own we set last year at $5 billion; Germany, recently, $7-2 billion; Italy, $3 billion; Netherlands, $2-82 billion. If you omit the smaller countries and their contributions- such as Luxembourg, Norway, Iceland, Portugal, Belgium and so on-you still have a total of some $213 billion previously approved.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For total defence.

For total defence, including Korea, domestic defence, NATO and every other form of defence. When we picked up the newspapers and read $300 billion for NATO defence, you can understand that most people were thunderstruck at the target the NATO nations had in mind. Of course it was not possible to contemplate the spending by these nations of even another $80 billion or $90 billion for all defence purposes. I suppose that Britain-indeed, I will not suppose it; I know that it is true-is in a better position economically than is either France or Italy. Yet within the last two weeks Mr. Churchill made it clear that his government could not fulfil in the three-year period the commitments made for defence by the previous government. He says that it will need at least four years to complete the three-year program which was adopted last year. Consequently one can readily understand that the budget published by the press was as misleading as it would have appeared to be phony if there had been any truth in it.

I can understand why the figure had been given, if for no other reason than perhaps to give our United States friends the idea that other nations were doing much more than they were doing or indeed could undertake.
I now want to say a word or two about something for which the minister took me to task last week. In the course of my remarks last week I asked him if he did not feel that the rearmament of Germany, before the integration of that country into the European family, would be disastrous. When the agreement was reached on Germany's financial contribution to rearmament and for the integration of the European defence community into NATO-and he explained that the European defence community would involve western Germany-surely it was not wrong to infer that agreements had been reached among the governments, of which Canada was one, even if the parliaments of, we will say, two or three of the nations did not subsequently ratify the agreements. I want to ask the minister this question. Is it not a fact that, as early as September, 1950, in New York the foreign ministers of France and Great Britain agreed to accept in principle the rearmament of western Germany? Was not a protocol even signed to that effect among them? Certainly an agreement was reached among them in principle. As the minister says, certain things are done in principle. I believe that was agreed upon in principle as early as in 1950. Why I raise this today is that I believe these suggestions for the rearmament of Germany have been and are dangerous to the rest of the world.
It is now reported, and authoritatively reported, that Russia is proposing, as part of a German unification plan, the remilitarization of Germany, setting up a German army, and granting the right to manufacture instruments of war and indeed the remilitarization to the extent that former German officers, even if they were former nazi officers, shall have the right to regain positions in the new German army. The Russians are proposing that the proposed army shall be free of association with any other army in Europe. If that is the case then it seems to me that the talk about the rearmament of Germany that we have been indulging in on our side has enabled the Russians to do something that is rather clever, and to outbid us for the support of the German people. We are now faced, and I think possibly Dr. Adenauer is faced, with a very difficult problem regarding the rearmament of Germany. It seems to me that the proposal for German rearmament had at its root of course the desire of the United States to withdraw as far as possible their own manpower from western Europe, and 55704-44
External Affairs
now the chickens are coming home to roost. I hope they will not be crows that will pick our bones again later on.
If I were to sum up what I have already said I could not do better than quote the London Economist in regard to these matters. In an article in the London Economist of March 1 last, I read these words:
It is a pity that NATO nowadays puts so much into the shop window without stating either the price or the quality of what it offers. During the Lisbon meeting of its council that ended this week statements were made to the press which were as woolly as the speeches of Gladstone's declining years.
Round figures, flat assertions, and high aspirations tumbled into print together, and it will need some plain speaking by Mr. Eden if the House of Commons is to get a clear and firm picture of the state of North Atlantic defence. It is right that a certain secrecy should surround NATO's diplomatic and military discussions, and that this should be proof even against the appalling inquisitiveness of congress. But to counterbalance this secrecy by talking airily of fifty divisions this year and a hundred in 1954, by giving the impression that the German defence contribution has been settled when it clearly has not, and by pretending that Franco-German difficulties over a European defence community are not so serious after all, is a dishonest practice. It will not frighten the Russians but it may well lull the Europeans. It is all very well to build up the prestige of NATO in American eyes: but if it is based on illusions there will be bitter disappointment one day.
That is the view I expressed in this house and our own national council expressed, and it caused us to use the words that the statement from Lisbon was irresponsible and disastrous. All this of course brings into sharp focus something to which the minister did not refer today, but I shall refer to it very briefly. I refer to the need for an attempt, and a continuous attempt, to reach a progressive disarmament agreement among the nations, and particularly with Russia. After all, the burden of rearmament must be as great on the Russian people as it is on the western nations.
If Mr. Churchill's recent statement, and indeed the statement of our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), that war is neither imminent nor inevitable is true-and I want to join them in saying that I think it is true -then with the strength we have already attained, every attempt should be made to clear up international disputes and reach agreements to disarm and build our common collective security through the United Nations.
They tried that at the end of the war.

This will be a difficult task, but we should turn down no opportunities, no matter how inadequate they appear to be, to achieve this result, and no matter how and by whom these offers are made.

External Affairs
The hon. gentleman interrupted me, but I am in good company when I say that.
We tried that since the war.

I am in good company when I say what I have just said. Let me quote Mr. Acheson. He made a statement on March 13. Of course he was calling attention to the forthcoming meeting in New York of the new United Nations disarmament commission, on which we have a representative, I believe. It began its meeting on March 14, last Friday, under the chairmanship, incidentally, of one of our own Canadian representatives, Mr. Johnson. This committee was established by the general assembly in Paris recently. This is what Mr. Acheson said. Some hon. gentlemen were inclined to laugh when I made the suggestion just now. Will they laugh at what the secretary of state in the United States said?

I was not laughing. We
have been trying to do that.

I did not say the hon.
member was laughing. Some others were. Mr. Acheson said:
It is not inconsistent to talk about reduction of armaments in this time of world tension and while we are still hard at work building our military strength.
We are rearming because we have been forced to do so by the threat to world peace and security stemming from the existence of huge armies and armaments in the Soviet Union and its satellites. But we are ready, as we have always been, to take the other and-from our viewpoint-much preferred way toward international peace and security: to cut down our forces if agreement can be reached on an effective plan of balanced disarmament.
We should keep that offer m our minds whenever we are discussing rearmament, as we were doing this afternoon. We should again turn our minds, as Mr. Acheson did, to the problem of disarmament. I am aware of the difficulties. I was present in 1946 when this matter was discussed before the general assembly in a very striking manner. I remember the atmosphere. I remember the hands of friendship that were stretched out to the representatives of the Soviet union by Sir Hartley Shawcross and by others, and I remember the manner in which the offers were spurned by the Soviet representative at that time, Mr. Molotov. But I say that whenever we are talking about rearmament we should not overlook the desirability of doing everything we can to promote disarmament.
Mr. Acheson said it was the business of the United Nations today to try to find a way to do that, and he added:
So that when the time is ripe nations may achieve international order without the burden of tremendous defence budgets.

As I said a moment ago, I know how difficult it is to discuss such matters with the communist representatives at the United Nations. Having sat and listened to them often enough I know that there are great difficulties. But sometimes I have thought this, that when something is suggested to our western delegations by the Russians, even though we have been inclined to suggest that proposal ourselves, it is not well received and, indeed, turned down.
A case in point, I think, was something that happened at the last assembly. I was sitting one evening at home listening to the radio, and I heard a press report from Paris in which it was stated that the Russians had suggested that all the nations that had not been admitted to the United Nations should be admitted as a bloc of nations. That was characterized as blackmail on the part of the Russians.
I remembered that before the committee on external affairs our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) had made that very suggestion. I looked up the record. Instead of summarizing what was said, I shall quote it. I asked him the question about the admission of certain nations to the United Nations, and the discussion that took place is to be found at page 64 of the official report of the proceedings of the committee on external affairs for the year 1950. It is as follows:

I think there is a growing
feeling that we should reopen this question of applications and let in everybody that applies. That would mean an admission of another thirteen or fourteen states which would include certain communist satellite states, but it would include Italy, Ireland, Portugal and other states which are not communist.
In fact, a majority of the states were not communist at that time.
My own view is that we should reconsider this whole question of applications and possibly accept all of them.
That seems sensible.
Would it be possible, Mr. Minister, to get around the Soviet veto?

Yes, I think it would be
possible. I do not want to be too dogmatic on anything the Russians may do but I think it would be possible if we said to Soviet Russia: we will accept all your nominees if you accept the other nominees. I think it would be possible to have them all admitted.
That, I thought, was a very sensible procedure. Yet, when the suggestion came before the general assembly at Paris we heard it characterized-and I hasten to say, not by the minister or by any Canadian officials, but rather by news services-as an attempt at blackmail on the part of the Russians. When it came to a vote, as I believe it did, we abstained, on this particular issue.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, we did.

Yes; and may I say to the minister that the Canadian delegation is getting quite a reputation for abstentions in the United Nations. Here was a case in point where, when something that has been acceptable to us is proposed by people we do not like, we do not support the proposal when it comes from that quarter. I think that is a mistake.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I ask a question? Would the hon. member read the list of states the Russians proposed for admission at that time?
I have not that list with me; but they are about the same as they were before.
Outer Mongolia.

There are two or three states to which I know we have objection-Outer Mongolia, for example. But there are some states to which they have objection, too. They might consider that some of these states are satellites of ours. And, after all, if you are making a horse trade you have to trade on the most advantageous basis possible. I do not think there has been any material change in the complexion this year of the number of nations from what there was in previous years.
I have felt that at times we have made a mistake in not giving consideration to suggestions that are made from the other side. And now, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might call it six o'clock, because I wish to say something about the Far Eastern situation, and this would seem to be the appropriate place to break off.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

I was ruled out of order last year for referring to this, but I might say that on October 9 last year a Gallup poll showed 73 per cent of Canadians in all walks of life as being entirely in favour of the adoption of the bill. The Victoria Colonist, which certainly is not favourable to me, has indicated its approval of this bill, as has the Edmonton chamber of commerce, the Toronto board of trade, the Brantford board of trade, the Vancouver News-Herald, the Vancouver Province, which wrote no less than three lead editorials, the national committee of the commercial travellers of Canada, the Financial Post, the Halifax board of trade, the Canadian tourist association, the Canadian chambers of commerce at their national convention, the Montreal Gazette, which wrote some lead editorials, the Montreal Herald and so on. The large labour organizations in Canada are 100 per cent in support of this bill.

Statutory Holidays
There is nothing intricate or devastating about the bill; it is most simple. It provides that instead of celebrating the 24th of May on the 24th of May or July 1 on July 1, those holidays will be celebrated on the following Monday. Last year July 1 fell on Sunday and by statute it was celebrated on the Monday. That resulted in a series of editorials and articles across Canada commending this bill. That gave the small man an opportunity to enjoy an unbroken week end.
We have royal precedent for changing the date of statutory holidays. Our late beloved sovereign, King George VI, decreed that his birthday should not be celebrated in December but in a more pleasant month during the summer. That in no way destroyed the attachment of the people of the United Kingdom or the commonwealth to their king, but it did give a greater opportunity to the subjects of His Majesty to enjoy the pleasures of a longer week end.
I do not wish to say much more about this matter. As was suggested, there has been a period of waiting and since the bill was first introduced we have had an opportunity to see what the reaction of the people of Canada was to a bill of this kind. I think I can leave the bill to the fair and impartial minds of this house to decide whether or not a measure universally acclaimed as this is, should be passed.
Not that this means the bill has any special merit, but in the thousands of instances in which I have personally discussed the matter with people I have not met anyone, with the exception of some of the members of the house, who is opposed to the adoption of this measure. There used to be an old saying that forty million Frenchmen can't be wrong. Surely 73 per cent of the people of Canada can't be all crazy. I would ask the house to consider this bill, to give it an opportunity of doing what three out of four people in Canada think it will do; that is, give them and their children a happier and more contented holiday week end from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) has put his case in support of this bill very fairly, and I should like to bring to the attention of my fellow members a few of the arguments against it. In effect this is a double-barrelled bill; it seeks to amend two statutes, in the first place the Dominion Day Act, which is chapter 49 of the revised statutes of 1927, and in the second place the Victoria Day Act, which is chapter 204 of the same statutes. The proposed amendment would set the holiday for the Monday following June 30, in the one instance, and for the Monday following May 23 in the other.
I think the argument of the hon. member may be summed up in these words: Give us two more long week ends. In effect that is the sum and substance of his argument. Tonight I am not going to deal particularly with the Victoria day holiday, but I do intend to refer to Dominion day, July 1. As we all know, July 1 is Canada's national birthday, our one truly national holiday. For many decades it has been celebrated as such. That is one of the fine traditions of this nation. Before we do away with this or any other tradition in this country I think we should have a great deal more reason than merely to bring about one more long week end.
This is a day we all celebrate, a day for Canadians of all origins, French-speaking Canadians, English-speaking Canadians and the hundreds of thousands of Canadians of other racial origins. This is one national tradition on which we all agree. It can be made something to draw us closer together. Why just throw it away, particularly at this time when we are welcoming to Canada many thousands of people from other parts of the world, people who I believe will have had national holidays in the countries from which they come? Surely we should keep our own national holiday for the benefit of those people, if for no other reason. It will help them learn to love this country of Canada.
Let us follow the example of our great and friendly neighbours, the Americans. They celebrate July 4; that is their great national holiday. Would anybody in this chamber be rash enough to say that the Americans would be willing to do away with their 4th of July and celebrate it on the nearest Monday? I suggest that the national spirit of the American people is so strong and they are such a proud people that they would never even consider such a suggestion. I think it is an indication of some lack in the spirit of the

Canadian people that they should give serious consideration to doing away with the Canadian national holiday on July 1.
If the change advocated by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is made, Canada will be asked to celebrate her national birthday on July 4 as often as she does on July 1. How ridiculous that would be. Take this year, 1952. If this bill should become law we would celebrate our national holiday on July 7; and if my calculations are correct we would not celebrate our national holiday on July 1 until 1957.
In many parts of the country we now have a five-day week. I know in British Columbia that is becoming almost universal. Even the lawyers are working on a five-day week, at least so it seems with the exception of my firm. Canadians who are on a five-day week have Saturday and Sunday free anyway. They now have a three-day week end if July 1 happens to fall on a Friday, a Sunday or a Monday. Already we have quite a few long week ends, and I do not know why we should be in such a great rush to get another. We have a long week end for the queen's birthday, another for Labour day and another for Thanksgiving day. If the change were made in connection with Victoria day, that would make four. Why should we go so far as to wipe out our national holiday in order to get a fifth long week end?
I suggest that if this bill is carried we will get one more long week end and lose our national holiday. Not only do I feel very strongly that this bill should not carry, and that we should not sacrifice our national holiday, but I believe we should take active steps to further the celebration of our national holiday. Other countries celebrate their national holidays. I remember when I was a youngster living in a small town in British Columbia we celebrated Victoria day and the adjoining town of Nelson celebrated July 1. I think that practice was universal throughout the whole of the Kootenay country. One town would celebrate one holiday, and another town the later one. They were great events, and certainly great days for the children in those communities. The result was that we had our attention focused on the nation and this helped build up in us great pride in Canada.
I believe that was a custom which should never have been abandoned. Just a few years ago we had an outstanding mayor in the city of Vancouver, Gerry McGeer, who as members know subsequently became a member of this house and then an hon. senator. As a matter of fact, he represented the riding of Vancouver-Burrard. While he was mayor he decided that Vancouver should
Statutory Holidays
revive her old practice of putting on a celebration on the first of July. Many people scoffed at the idea and said, "Oh, we want to go away for a week end; we are not going to stay in the city to take part in a celebration which is just a lot of poppycock." But Gerry did not allow himself to be influenced by the people who took that attitude. We all know what great energy he had, and what an organizer he was. He went ahead and put on a first-class show. Not only the residents of Vancouver but thousands of people from the surrounding territory turned out for this celebration, and saw a bang-up first of July national holiday celebration which did a great deal of good to everyone who was there.
I believe that the leadership should come from members in this house in promoting celebrations of that kind on our national holiday. We would be much wiser to be trying to work out plans for such celebrations than to be trying to work out some way in which to get rid of the holiday and get a long week end. This question is important now, Mr. Speaker, but it is going to be more important as the years go by. These traditions will mean more and more to Canada. Today we have one day on which we can all unite; a tradition which helps to build up the national spirit of this country. I do hope that this house will not take the backward step of doing away with Dominion day in order that we can get one more long week end.

I think
it is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that in our language we have only the one word "holiday" to describe occasions with widely different meaning. A holiday may be a day of pleasure and relaxation, or it may be a day dedicated to solemn remembrance. Civic holiday in August is an example of the former, and Christmas day is an example of the latter. It would destroy the meaning of Christmas if we were to change the celebration of that day to suit our convenience. On the other hand, it would be foolish not to change the civic holiday date if we so wished, because that holiday was instigated purely for our pleasure.
I do not believe that Dominion day and Victoria day should be considered together because they are holidays that have very different reasons for existing. Victoria day celebrates the birthday of that great queen, and was given to the people of the commonwealth as a day for pleasure and relaxation.
Dominion day, on the other hand, commemorates the most significant event in the history of this country. The holiday that

Statutory Holidays
celebrates Dominion day is a most important day, and I think it is one on which we must remember the very important event that happened 85 years ago on July 1. It was never meant to be merely a cheerful break in the routine of our lives.
Victoria day was given as a holiday to be simply cheerful and relaxing in the routine of our lives. In that case the important thing is not the date. Some people may attach importance to Victoria day and feel that it should remain on May 24, but there are many precedents for changing the birthday of a monarch so that the celebration can be a holiday for the people. Edward VII changed the celebration of his birthday; so did George VI and recently our present monarch, Queen Elizabeth II, changed the celebration of her birthday from April to June 9 so that the people could enjoy a holiday at a more pleasant time of year.
With these precedents before us, I say let us change the celebration of Victoria day to the Monday immediately before May 24 so that the people may derive the greatest benefit from that holiday. I say the Monday before May 24 because the queen's birthday is to be celebrated on June 9, and I think it is advisable to keep the two holidays a reasonable distance apart.
Industrial workers have very few opportunities to take their families away for a holiday. A long week end in May would give them this opportunity at one of the nicest times of the year. When they get a holiday in the middle of the week, there is very little that working people can do, especially those with large families. They simply have to spend the holiday in or near their own neighbourhood, with very little benefit to themselves or families.
Now, if the holiday is added to the week end, those in industrial areas can take their families into the country to visit relatives and friends, or go to the cottage, as so many people do today if the holiday happens to fall on a Monday or Friday. This means a very real holiday for working people. The same thing applies to people living in the country, because they get a chance to visit the cities and towns, and enjoy a temporary change.
I think it is important for people to be able to get away from their usual surroundings once in a while. The more opportunities we can provide for them to do so, the more everyone will benefit. Victoria day was meant for everybody's pleasure, and therefore if that day is changed to the Monday before May 24 people could make plans to
IMr. Hees.l
derive the maximum benefit from that holiday. I therefore hope that section 2 of this bill will be passed. But, Mr. Speaker, I believe that the Dominion day holiday is a different matter. It commemorates a solemn national event and the holiday on July 1 has become a precious national tradition. I should be loath to see this holiday removed from the significance of its special date. It would then become indistinguishable in importance from the August Civic holiday and the September Labour day, and would be just another holiday.
I believe that Dominion day should remain a special day. It should be a kind of solemn rededication to our country and, as such, I believe it should be as immovable as Christmas. As to the Victoria day, Civic holiday and Labour day, it is the happy holiday that counts, not the day; hence they may be arranged to make them the best and most convenient holidays possible. As to Dominion day, it is the day, and the significance of that particular day, that counts.
Let us therefore not belittle our great national day by changing it to meet our convenience and pleasure. Rather let us set aside this particular day to remember with thanksgiving the founding of our nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a few remarks that I should like to make with regard to the principle involved in deciding which date we should choose in the case of our public holidays. Should we govern our thoughts mainly by tradition or should we bow to convenience? In this case I think that the purpose of the bill is to arrange to have these holidays fall on a Monday so that two more long week ends could be provided. That suggestion has a great deal of merit, as has been pointed out by the hon. members who have already spoken. Nevertheless, I think we are in danger of becoming too practical and of forgetting the great traditions which are the cement which hold us together as a nation. These holidays should remind us of the great traditions which we follow and of the great heritage which is ours as a free and democratic people.
Six years ago I had the honour and the pleasure of representing this country in an informal and quite happy way in the south of France where Victoria day was first celebrated. I refer to the town of Aix-les-Bains where Queen Victoria used to go for her holidays in the summer, and where Victoria day was celebrated for many years before ever it was celebrated anywhere in the British empire under that name. This experience made me realize the value of those traditions of which we are reminded when we celebrate our national holidays. I

saw there what that day meant for the people of that community and the great importance they attached to it; I found that it was a symbol of their attachment for the British people and for the cause of freedom which we fought together to defend during the last war.
In the town square there is a monument of Queen Victoria. It consists of a bronze bust of the queen. When that part of France was occupied, the French maquis or underground workers risked their lives in order to save that monument and to bury it until France was again liberated. I had the pleasure of being present when that monument was reinstalled in the town square in that delightful little town in the south of France. It made me realize that I had seen Victoria day celebrated in a much better and more noteworthy fashion than I had ever seen it celebrated in Canada. It made me realize that perhaps we take these holidays of ours somewhat too lightly, that we forget their real significance, and tend to let our children do likewise.
As the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) has pointed out, I think we could afford to be practical enough, in the case of Victoria day, to let the day on which the birthday of Queen Victoria is celebrated be flexible enough so that it would fall on a Monday and thereby provide an additional long week end for the people in the cities. Incidentally, I may say that it would give the hon. member who sponsored this bill-I refer to the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall)-the opportunity to go to Victoria on Victoria day, if he saw fit to do so.
But when we come to Dominion day, I think we would be making a poor move to consider celebrating it on any other day than the first of July. After all, if the event has any significance at all it should be celebrated on the day that gives it its significance. I do not believe that we would be wise in celebrating confederation on any other day than the first day of July. After all, we would think it exceedingly strange if the people of the United States decided to celebrate the fourth of July on the seventh of July or something of that kind.
