speechtext: It being nine o'clock, we snail return to the business before the house at the dinner recess.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of supply.

Mr. Speaker, just to complete the record, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) asked me before the dinner recess the names of the nations that might have been admitted, had the first committee approved of the resolution recommending them all to the security council. I have those names before me, and I find that they are Albania, Mongolia, Bulgaria, Roumania, Hungary, Finland, Italy, Portugal, Ireland, Jordan, Austria, Ceylon and Nepal. They were also asked to consider Libya's application. I take it that the group of nations would not have been less favourable from our point of view than the group we were discussing in 1950.
I said at six o'clock that I wished to say something about the Far Eastern situation, and particularly something further because of the remark of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) regarding the Korean armistice negotiations. I suggested a week ago that, the Korean armistice negotiations now having spread over a period of nine months, it might be well to consider getting together the political representatives of the nations actually engaged in war in Korea, to see if an armistice could not be reached in that way. I did that because I felt that there was a stalemate, and some fresh attempt

should be made to break it. In my view that was a positive suggestion, particularly as the hon. member for Peel had suggested that we should not take negative positions in connection with international affairs. And, after all, having achieved the original objective which, as the minister pointed out this afternoon, was to drive the aggressors beyond the 38th parallel, we I think could afford to negotiate an armistice at the earliest possible moment-because I think all the nations are tired of the stalemate in Korea.
I know that it is a bit risky to discuss the Far Eastern situation, and particularly if one feels that once matters in Korea are settled an attempt should be made to obtain a general settlement in the Far East. People who have said that are described as fellow travellers, communists and so on. I am sorry to say that in our neighbouring country, the United States, some people have almost been silenced on that account. Recently we have noted the manner in which Mr. Owen Latti-more, for example, has been pilloried before the senate committee. Five years ago he warned his country that Chiang Kai-shek was out, that the Chinese people would have nothing further to do with him. Like General Marshall he said that they should endeavour to find democratic personnel in China and support that personnel in the formation of a government, or failing that to endeavour to get a coalition government, which would perhaps have some communist representatives, that would prevent the country falling into the arms of the communist leaders in China.
Unfortunately support for the corrupt regime now in Formosa drove the Chinese literally into the arms of .the Soviet union and upset the balance in Asian affairs, to which the hon. member for Peel referred this afternoon, and jeopardized the leadership which democratic India might have given to the Asian people. There was a possibility of bringing the Asian people as a whole to our side after the statesmanlike manner in which self-government was granted to India, Pakistan and Ceylon and the manner in which subsequently Indonesia was granted self-government. I am glad to see that the new government of Great Britain under Mr. Churchill, despite the fact that Mr. Churchill once said that he did not wish to preside over the liquidation of the British empire, is following the same policy in the Far East which his predecessors followed. As a matter of fact, in yesterday's papers there was a dispatch from Malaya quoting the new British high commissioner, General Sir Gerald Templer, as having called for the extension of common citizenship to Malaya's two million Chinese

and six hundred thousand Indians, and other measures leading to more self-government for this British country. He stated further that the emergency cannot be fought by military measures alone.
That is exactly what we have been saying in this House of Commons ever since the difficulties arose with the Soviet union. If we want to contain-I do not like the expression- communism, it cannot be done by military means alone. The minister has stated again and again that economic aid is a weapon that we must use. My criticism of the minister and the government to some extent is that insufficient attention has been given to article 2 of the NATO agreement, the Colombo plan and to Point Four of Mr. Truman's statement regarding aid to backward peoples.
I think much more attention has to be paid to that if we are to win the world to our democratic way of life. The Asian peoples are determined to throw off the age-old domination and exploitation by their own domestic reactionary rulers or representatives of imperialistic power. No military aid that we give to the reactionary elements in Indochina or anywhere else in the Far East will help us and our views. We shall play into the hands of the Soviet union unless we take other steps to meet the crisis that faces the world in the Far East.
Because of the fear of Soviet imperialism the democratic powers have been supporting reactionary regimes like that of the Syngman Rhee in South Korea. While we are not engaged in a war to put Syngman Rhee back in power, nonetheless there are elements among us who look upon that as a solution to the Korean situation. Then there is Chiang Kai-shek, and so on. The people of Asia are determined to throw off their bonds and we should be giving much more attention to this side of the problem than we have.
If there is any disillusionment among the Chinese people at the present time, and I think there may be, regarding their new communist rulers, we certainly cannot expect any support from the Chinese for the return of Chiang Kai-shek. Certainly we should have no part in any such attempt, nor do I believe from what the minister said today that Canada intends to give any support to a solution of the Chinese problem of that description.
It seems to me that all the western nations, including Canada, should endeavour once the Korean matter is brought to an end to find a settlement that will do two things. First, give the Asian peoples an opportunity of choosing their own forms of government. We cannot dictate to them what that form of government shall be.
External Affairs

How are
the Chinese people to form their own government?
As a matter of fact, they have chosen sides now.
How have they chosen?

They drove out Chiang Kai-shek in spite of the fact that he had billions of dollars' worth of equipment from our nations, particularly from the United States, and at one time had as many as eight million men under arms. Yet he had to leave the mainland of China-I will put it that way- and find refuge on the island of Formosa. Consequently I think it is logical to assume that even if the present government of China obtained complete control of that country by force of arms, nonetheless the majority of the people supported the victors over the former regime in China.
Where does Russia come in?

My hon. friend wants to know where Russia comes in. Probably Russia helped to arm the Chinese, but a large part of their armour came from our countries. This had been delivered into their hands by the Chinese soldiers of Chiang Kai-shek who wanted to overthrow his corrupt regime. Indeed many of the weapons bear the marks of North American factories. That is where many of the arms came from.
I agree with those people who believe that neither the Soviet union, the United States nor any other power will eventually control China. China never has been controlled by a foreign power. China never will be controlled by an outside nation. The Chinese people themselves will eventually settle the form of government which they will have in China. In any event we should not be a party to using young Canadian lives, weapons of war or our resources in a hopeless endeavour to inflict the Chiang Kai-shek regime upon the Chinese people once again. That is the point I am making; and I say it is generally true throughout Asia that the people are on the march, determined to achieve selfgovernment.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to deal with several other matters in connection with international affairs. I would have liked to say a word about the Middle East.
Go ahead.

No. Some other opportunity will present itself, and I always try to remain within the time allotted to a private member of parliament.

External Affairs

Mr. Speaker, I always approach these external affairs debates with some trepidation, because I realize how easy it is in the heat of debate on such matters to say something that might be interpreted as perhaps dangerous to the unity of the Canadian people in regard to the policy the government wishes to follow in connection with the relationship of Canada to the other nations of the world. It is because I feel my responsibility in that matter that I very often approach these debates with some misgivings. I am quite sure, however, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) was sincere and earnest when he said he wanted the position of each party on the opposition side of the house set forth clearly, and I think he is entitled to know just exactly where we stand. I also think he is entitled to have us say what we feel in language that is not diplomatic. I could not use that kind of language anyhow, so I will just have to be as blunt as usual.
I think it should be recognized, Mr. Speaker, that no matter how much unity we may have as to the fundamental principles of our external affairs policy, there is an area for fairly comprehensive discussion and indeed for some criticism of details within the boundaries of those principles. I do not think the minister would expect us to conduct ourselves otherwise than in a critical way if we feel there are criticisms to be offered or suggestions to be made. I have always found him ready to take a look at those criticisms at any rate. If in anything I say I do sound critical I want the minister to know that it is not with a view to making his job more difficult than it is. I am sincere in that. I want him to know that I would not consciously do anything to make it harder for him to carry forward the job he is undertaking to do in the international sphere. He represents Canada. He is our spokesman in most of our international relationships. He wants to know what the Canadian people are thinking, and one way he can get to know that is by listening to what we have to say here in this house.
With that as a background I would like to proceed to tell the minister just how we regard some of the matters he brought into the debate this afternoon, to tell him where we stand with regard to Korea and the Far East, let us say; with regard to China and these other things. We stand, as we have stood from the beginning, in support of the objectives adopted by the United Nations as stated by the minister himself on various occasions, relative to the situation in Korea and the Far East. I hold in my hand a

document coming from the fifth session of the United Nations general assembly, and from page 2 of this document I read a resolution which was adopted by the assembly on October 7, 1950, I understand by a very large majority. This is the part I wanted to quote:
Recalling that the essential objective of the resolutions of the general assembly referred to above was the establishment of a unified, independent and democratic government of Korea (the assembly) recommends that
(a)	all appropriate steps be taken to ensure conditions of stability throughout Korea;
(b)	all constituent acts be taken, including the holding of elections, under the auspices of the United Nations, for the establishment of a unified, independent and democratic government in the sovereign state of Korea;
(c)	all sections and representative bodies of the population of Korea, south and north, be invited to co-operate with the organs of the United Nations in the restoration of peace, in the holding of elections and in the establishment of a unified government;
In a speech at the plenary session of the United Nations assembly on September 27, 1950, the minister himself had this to say; and I quote from page 2 of the white paper containing the documents on the Korean crisis:
In the first place, the general objective as we see it of the United Nations in Korea should be to fulfil now the purposes which have repeatedly been stated at previous assemblies-a united Korea, a free Korea, a Korea which the Korean people themselves govern without interference from outside. This should be achieved by United Nations action and not through decisions reached by certain of its members.
In our judgment these statements of objectives are clear and unequivocal. But this afternoon the minister spoke as though the objective now is merely to defeat aggression. The question I have to ask, therefore, is: have we backed down from our original purpose, namely to establish a free, unified, independent and democratic government of Korea? I am sure the members of this house can distinguish between putting down aggression in Korea, which was the subject of the minister's talk this afternoon, and on the other hand achievement of the objective set out by the United Nations assembly and by the minister himself before the plenary session on September 27, 1950.
If we have backed down, if the United Nations Organization is going to be satisfied merely to stabilize the situation by agreeing to a dividing line let us say at the 38th parallel, would that be achieving the objective as set out by the United Nations? What about the armistice negotiations? If those negotiations which are going on right now should fail, then I ask how can we hope to achieve the objective as decided upon by the assembly without having the armies of the United Nations advance to the Yalu river and there

stabilize their position? Beyond that point how far must the United Nations go? Is it going to be necessary to go as far, let us say, as to bomb and destroy the Manchurian bases and accumulation points in order to secure their position at the Yalu river?
I know that when such things are mentioned they cause considerable hysteria amongst certain people. We are warned that if such action as the bombing of bases beyond the Yalu river were taken, it would inevitably bring us into an all-out war with China. Well, something that has been pretty hard for me to understand right from the beginning is this. We all knew that if we did intervene in Korea we would run a chance, right from the beginning, of coming into conflict with China. Why did that not stop us then, if we were unwilling to run the chance involved in fulfilling our obligations under the United Nations charter and the assembly's resolution? That is a question that requires an answer.
Now, to make our position clear, we believe that the United Nations should make every effort to achieve the objective as laid down in the assembly's resolution of October, 1950. What means they propose to take to achieve it, we shall have to leave to the United Nations and their command. We must say that no policy of a limited war for an unlimited period of time, according to our view, will ever achieve that objective.
I turn for a moment to the question of recognition of the Peiping regime in China. I think that the western nations made some terrible blunders in dealing with China during world war II, and especially after that war closed. Had there been the slightest good judgment amongst the advisers to the top men of the leading nations of the world, and had there been an honest effort directed towards this end, China would not be in the hands of the reds. But there she is. The Peiping regime certainly-I support the minister in this statement-should not be allowed to shoot its way into membership in the United Nations. Those are the words he used.
Nobody wishes that.

No. Nor, indeed, should they be allowed to shoot their way into recognition by other nations. But let us make it abundantly clear that when we are taking that position it is the communist leaders and their aggressive and inhuman policies which we resist and dislike, and not the Chinese people. The door should not be closed between the decent, freedom loving and intensely nationalistic Chinese peoples and the West. Indeed, the western nations ought to use every effort within their power to get over to these people our sincere desire to
External Affairs
assist them, if we can, to become liberated from the tyrannist dictatorship under which they have fallen, and to raise the standard of living of the Chinese people. Those things we must get over to them.
I come now to Formosa. We would strenuously oppose the return of Chiang Kai-shek and his army to the mainland at this time. We believe that the United Nations should defend Formosa and prevent it from falling into communist hands. Certainly, we should not hand over that island to the Peiping regime. What happens to Formosa after peace has been restored and through proper negotiations is another thing, but that represents our position. There are a good many people, Mr. Speaker, who feel that upon the outbreak of aggression in Korea it might have been better for the western nations to have established a line somewhere between the groups of islands making up the Japanese group and Formosa and the mainland, instead of intervening in Korea. These people may have some good points in their arguments to the effect that under such circumstances it would have only been a naval operation. Of course, it is too late to talk about that now. If a blunder has been made, it has been made and we have to try to correct it somehow.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with respect to Lisbon. I am glad I waited to find out a little more about the press report and what actually was contained in it before I said anything. I have never yet listened myself into trouble, but I have seen many people talk themselves into it. I think the minister has had an experience now perhaps that might be good for him, and in the future I suppose press liaison officers will be more careful about how they issue statements. To come back to the outcome of NATO, I am speaking entirely for the moment of military objectives. We support the military objectives as they were made somewhat more clear by the minister this afternoon, but we do object strenuously to what appears to be, in all too many quarters, only a half-hearted effort to make ready to successfully defend the free Atlantic nations against an aggressor or combination of aggressors. There are a good many people throughout the world who are feeling this way. I picked up the last two issues of U.S. News and World Report. I do not know how many millions of people this publication represents, but I know there are a good many millions who read it and will be influenced by this sort of thing. Listen to what it has to say on page 8 of the issue for March 21:
Armament is to become more and more a pumppriming project-

External Affairs
Every now and then you have to inject something into the bloodstream of the economy, so they start the old armament pump.
How do you spell that word?
Pump-priming?
Oh, yes, pump-priming. With a hyphen?

Yes, that is right, with a hyphen. The article continues:
Arms money tends to be turned on or off, to be directed this way or that way, depending on economic weather vanes. Armament, as the planners set it, can become a great stabilizer of the future.
Does that mean to say that we have to go on indefinitely priming the pump, and not attempting to come to any conclusion with respect to the struggles that are going on? Just let them go on as a sort of stabilizing influence? Is that the idea-a limited war for a limited period of time?
The article continues:
Arms race is something of a phony. Instead of sprinting to get arms with which to win, attention is on jogging along, using arms money to keep business on a fairly even keel. Economic effects and opportunities in arms are getting more official attention of planners than the military effects.
The planners figure that they've really got something in arms money.
This is United States opinion right within the nation that is supposed to be leading the nations of the world today. We are supposed to be following this nation. Then they say:
War itself obviously is to go on simmering. War tempo in Korea will remain slow. Bigger war is not intended. Blockade for China seems vetoed as of now. Bombing of China as well.
And so on. We can hardly be blamed, Mr. Speaker, ini the light of such things as this for wondering if the haste to get into Korea back in June 1950 might have been because a lot of the planners saw some economic depression in the offing. The old pump has to be primed.
Then I turn to page 45 of the issue of March 14, and I read this because it does support the idea of a simmering war about which I have talked.
It is a strange kind of arms race, this one between Russia and the west. It begins to look as if only one side is really running.
After the invasion of Korea set off the race, some twenty months ago . . . Russia, at the start, had the troops, tanks, planes to sweep across Europe, go deep into Asia. Russia now has many more tanks and planes-plus A-bombs.
The west, at the start, didn't even have enough to stop invasion of Korea or Indo-China, let alone halt Soviet sweeps across Europe or the Middle East.
The west, now, after 20 months of the arms race, can hold in Korea but not win, and still lacks forces in being to turn back a Soviet invasion of Europe.

As the west is running this race . . . Britain is tiring on the first lap, cutting its speed by a third, taking four years to cover a three-year course. France, limping badly, has stumbled on the first turn. Western Germany, counted on heavily, isn't even in the race yet. U.S., far out. in front with the dollars, appears to be talking a better race than it is running. U.S. is lagging, too.
Mr. Speaker, it is not I who say those things. That is criticism being published in a prominent magazine which comes from the United States. Can a person therefore be wondered at if he begins to express some concern about the sincerity of purpose being displayed by those nations which are supposed to be out there doing their level best to build up a defensive arrangement, an integrated army in western Europe?
I fear that the western nations have not. been and are not now taking advantage of the breathing spell which Providence has granted to them within which to get themselves ready to meet the dangers that we have seen coming for a long while. I do not know whether we shall ever be able to make up that time, but the speed at which we seem to be going would indicate that we have lost most valuable time. The real danger, in my judgment, is that time will run out before we are ready. If we are going to take collective action-and we want to see collective action of such magnitude as is required for the safety of these nations, including Canada-then we have got to shake off uncertainties, or any diffidence that is besetting us, and must plunge into the preparations with all our energy. This warning applies to the leader nations, more especially the United States and Canada; but, Mr. Speaker, while we support and urge strong defence-defence which is just as strong as we need to turn back any aggressor or combination of aggressors-we at this time want to utter a few words of caution.
We think that every effort will have to be made to cushion our economy against the terrible impact of defence and other demands that are being made upon it. That statement holds true, I suppose, for other nations in the world, particularly those that are within the NATO group. We think that care will have to be exercised to see to it that we do not destroy productive incentive- that is, the incentive to produce in an all-out fashion-within our own country, by imposing on our people heavy taxation that they just cannot bear. There is no necessity for it. It can be financed in other ways. We ought to induce all-out productive effort by every good policy that can be laid down. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that therein lies a realm for some serious criticism of this government. They are not offering the proper inducement

'to all-out production, especially of foods; and foods are a vital necessity in this war against communism.
My colleagues the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) already this session have put on the record some vital and potent material with respect to their views and our views in connection with the importance of food in the winning of this struggle. If we take a realistic view of the situation, we are going to note that the farmers of this country are ready to make that all-out effort to produce food in abundance, as we can produce it, if we assure the farmers that there will be a market for it.
At a fair price.

Yes, at what to them represents a fair price. But the farmers take a realistic view and they say this: What is the use of making such an effort if the markets are not there? We can-and I am sure that everybody who knows the situation will agree-substantially increase our production of foodstuffs and we can set up that kind of organization that will distribute those foodstuffs into the hands of people, within this country and in other countries, that can use them and that need them.
My colleague the hon. member for Acadia the other night, speaking in this house, impressed upon the members three steps that he thought we should take. May I just take one moment to review them. It appears to me that this is one of the things that we have got to keep in our minds as we make this defensive effort to try to build ourselves into a strength sufficient to resist aggressors.
The first thing the hon. member for Acadia impressed upon us was this. He said that we can find a ready market for much of our surplus agricultural produce right here in Canada if we see to it that every Canadian is given the opportunity to consume a fair amount of our production; in other words, if we see to it that he has a decent living. Thousands of our people, he pointed out, are today not getting sufficient in view of these high prices which prevail; and he was referring to those people who have to live on fixed small incomes, as many of them have to do. There is within our own country an almost unlimited market for much of our agricultural products.
The second thing he pointed out was this. In so far as we cannot market our own produce in Canada or exchange it for the goods of other nations, we must be prepared to sell our surplus to other nations in exchange for their currencies, and not haggle about the necessity for convertibility, which
External Affairs
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) tried to shove down the throats of the people at the conference that was held in London not long ago. By demanding that everything be done on the basis of convertibility, he forced Britain to cut back her exports by one-third. That is not the way to do business. We ought to be prepared to accept their currency. Someone may say: What good will that currency do us? In reply I would say: Maybe not any immediately. But the third point that the hon. member for Acadia stressed was this, and it is a practical one. To the extent that those currencies cannot be spent for goods which we would want to bring back and consume in Canada, we must be prepared to invest those currencies within the countries-like Britain and other countries-that want our goods, in order to expand their production so that they will be in a position to pay for their imports with exports, eventually; and that course would redound to our advantage.
There is plenty of scope within which to develop markets for the products of our farms as an incentive to all-out productive effort. Then we can look to the Colombo plan and other economic-aid programs to take some of the production of food which we are capable of producing and are willing to produce in these days. Much has been said about the Colombo plan and our participation in it. Last year we gave something like $25 million to assist in the technical aid or Colombo plan program. I do not yet know just exactly the details of how it was spent. I do not know just how much the other nations gave. I have not been able to get the details of that as yet. Perhaps they are available. There is, however, one thing that I want to say. We supported that contribution of $25 million to the Colombo plan, but we thought it was only a drop in the bucket as compared with the needs of the people of the world. Hungry people are the finest soil for communism and its growth.
There is one thing that I should like to mention in connection with our assistance under the Colombo plan.
Before my hon. friend proceeds, may I ask him a question?
Yes, indeed.

With regard to the payment for Canadian goods in foreign currency, would he be ready to recommend the acceptance of Spanish pesetas in payment of Canadian goods, and would he add Spain to the list of countries which has been read by the previous speakers, and which should be admitted to NATO?

External Affairs

I certainly think that we should be prepared to expand our trade with Spain on an even basis with every other country that wants to trade with us and that would mean the acceptance of their currency, if that is all they have to offer us at the moment. If by accepting that currency there is any hope of obtaining increased production within Spain out of which they could buy or pay for our goods sometime in the near future, then we should do so.
Exactly.

Yes, I certainly will agree; but as far as admitting Spain to the United Nations is concerned, I cannot understand anybody who will fight against Spanish membership in the United Nations and yet be prepared to accept Russia, Czechoslovakia, Poland and those others.
Very good.
It is something I cannot understand. If I were going to fight against a membership in the United Nations I would fight it on a principle, and not on my prejudices.
You have no prejudices.
I hope not in this respect, and I hope that I can rid myself of prejudices.
You have just proved that you have none.

I said that within the realm of NATO we have to consider not only the military program but the non-military. So far as we in this group are concerned, we support any realistic non-military program for the closer co-operation of the nations making up NATO, and also, Mr. Speaker, any organization, in such a way as to get food into the stomachs of hungry people and help to lift them out of the slough of despond into which they have been thrust by circumstances.
There is one thing further I want to mention in connection with the Colombo plan. I hold in my hand one of the international conciliation booklets put out by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. I am reading at this moment from page 3 a little statement made by Trygve Lie, secretary general of the United Nations. It is in an article written by Dr. Arnold G. Huth, who appears to be somewhat of an authority on this particular phase of the work of the Colombo plan. This is Mr. Trygve Lie's statement:
I believe that the whole technical assistance program will depend to a great extent for its lasting success on the degree of confidence and support that it can command at the local community level and its ability to stimulate local action.

This is obviously true, but Dr. Huth says this:
The degree of confidence in the technical assistance program and the degree of support by the people largely depend upon the understanding and approval of the program, and thus upon the use made of the media of communications and information. The words of the secretary-general of the United Nations, spoken at the opening session of the general conference of UNESCO in Paris, in June, 1951, thus emphasize the importance of communications in economic development.
It has become more and more evident that the greatest obstacle to the technical assistance program is perhaps not the lack of funds and equipment but rather the lack of interest and support by public opinion, frequently indifferent, ignorant or hostile. How can this problem be solved as long as the media of communications necessary to inform and to arouse public opinion are so deficient, particularly in those areas where they are most needed?
Dr. Huth goes on to make a comparison of the communications in the underdeveloped areas of the world with those in the highly developed areas such as the United States. I was amazed when I saw this:
While the United States has 40,709,389 telephones, India with more than twice as many inhabitants has only 128,911 telephones. Indonesia with seventy-eight million inhabitants only 35,750 telephones and Pakistan with seventy-five million, only 17,445.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: They are probably much happier.

Yes; I can imagine that the minister oftentimes feels that he would like to take his off the wall and throw it in the waste-paper basket. I often do myself. But I think on more careful thought we would hate to do without them. I can imagine how much more tired the minister would be if he had to hop around to wherever his voice can be thrown in two or three minutes. It just points out, however, Mr. Speaker, the vast difference between the United States and many of these underdeveloped parts of the world when it comes to trying to get information out to the people to remove whatever prejudice or opposition there may be in their minds toward assistance from other countries, particularly when we are trying, under the technical assistance program, to go into these underdeveloped areas and help them to help themselves. If we run up against opposition we have to depend upon communication to educate the people, and that is one of the things that have not been done. Unfortunately we have not attended to the basic things first, and this may be one of the reasons why these technical assistance programs have been so slow in taking hold.
A further comparison, Mr. Speaker:
The United States has 1,773 daily newspapers with a total circulation of 54,017,938 copies, Saudi Arabia has not a single daily newspaper.

When the minister issues his communique from Lisbon he has not one newspaper in Saudi Arabia. Perhaps he wishes there were only one in Canada. I continue:
The United States has 19,796 motion picture theatres with 12,384,150 seats, as contrasted with 4 cinemas, seating 2,500 people, in Afghanistan. The United States has 2,890 broadcasting and 108 television stations; in many countries there are only one or two radio stations.
And so the contrast goes. Dr. Huth sums up in this way:
While problems of transportation have received a great deal of attention during the last few years and increasing efforts are being made for their expansion and improvement, problems of communications-mass communications in particular-have been almost entirely neglected in the plans and programs for economic development and technical assistance. It is true that some countries have requested audio-visual specialists and that the projects for fundamental education include some provisions for the use of mass media. But the whole question of mass communications in underdeveloped areas-and more particularly the problem of public information through the mass media -is still largely unexplored.
If we are really going to do the job of the Colombo plan we shall have to start with first things first and undertake to improve the communications so that we can get over to the masses of the people that we intend to do some good, and then we will remove that opposition and perhaps the Colombo plan can be expanded. But Canada is in a position to do more than she has done. Perhaps the minister will say that we did not do more last year because of that very thing, the fact that there was not a chance to spend the money any more quickly under the circumstances.
Well, we ought to take that into consideration, if we are ever inclined to criticize the minister. But there is one thing certain, that through better methods of trade, more sensible trading arrangements, we must also get out into fields of assistance by way of such things as the Colombo plan, if we ever expect to help underdeveloped countries of the world and to raise their standard of living. And Canada is in a position to be of real help to them.
Now, I have only one more observation to make. Let me sum up briefly in one sentence or two our position: We support any sensible and realistic effort by NATO to build up adequate defences in western Europe. We do say, though, that the people of the various NATO countries have every right to be informed, in the utmost detail consistent with safety, of all those things that the council decide, and which the NATO organization undertakes to do.
External Affairs
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have not taken note of the time left at my disposal. However, I have only one more point to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has now exceeded his time.
Very well; I shall just leave it at that. There will be another occasion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

I certainly do not wish to impose upon the time of the house. However, there is one thing I had thought I would like to say briefly, because I believe it is of great importance and has not yet been mentioned either this afternoon or this evening in the debate.
I am not one who believes that a third world war is inevitable, or that a third world war is the only means of dividing or destroying communism. I certainly am not. As a matter of fact I am convinced that world conflict would be the very means of spreading the virus of communism into those parts of the world which are not now so seriously affected by it.
What has been the history of the past? What has been the experience of the past? Well, world war I thoroughly established communism as a world movement, and gave it a motherland-Russia. World war II provided an opportunity and a means for the spread of communist influence into all parts of the world, and for the unfolding of imperialistic designs of the communist leaders in Russia. Those same leaders have now at least partially achieved their primary objective-that is, the objective they set first- namely that of uniting all the proletariat of industrial Germany, Austria and Czechoslovakia with those of Russia, the object being of course to create a mighty, industrial-agricultural combination that would stretch from Vladivostok in the east to the Rhine in the west, and from the gulf of Finland in the north to the Danube in the south.
This they dreamed of as a self-supporting and terrible front, capable of withstanding the capitalistic countries of the west. Now the ultimate goal of course is world dictatorship under Soviet rule. They hope that such a thing will emerge as the result of a third world war; if that should come. It appears to be the aim of Russia, the aim of Russian communist leaders-and	I differentiate
between Russian communist leaders and the Russian people, because we ought to make

External Affairs
it known that we are not fighting the Russian people, but that we are opposed to the Bolshevik leaders and their program of imperialistic expansion-I say it appears to be the aim of communist leaders to bring on a war at a time and under circumstances of their own choosing.
While their satellites have become nuisance spots in different parts of the world, it is the aim of course of the Russian leaders to capitalize on the weaknesses of the western world, and on the hunger and discontent of the southeast Asiatic countries, and the spread of communist influence far and wide.
In his message to congress, and dealing with what has come to be known as a mutual security program, the President of the United States said that there are only two alternatives, namely premeditated and deliberate war, or an American withdrawal to the western hemisphere.
I would not like the Secretary of State for External Affairs to share that view. For that reason we in this group at various times have warned the government not to allow themselves to be too much influenced by the American attitude. I say there are other alternatives to that of premeditated and deliberate war on the one hand or withdrawal into isolation within the western hemisphere by the United States.
I say there are other alternatives. Evidently President Truman does not see a third area within which real and earnest effort ought to be made to defeat communism and to establish the world under a rule of lasting peace. And it is that third area, that area of negotiation and of most careful psychological effort to get to and to influence the many millions of people behind the iron curtain who are still determined to regain liberty, and to let them know that we are their friends and are interested in helping to liberate them-I say it is within that third area where we can do so much by way of economic aid and technical assistance.
We have not begun to explore the possibilities within that third area. I say that that is an area in which today we ought to be most interested. If we are not, then I am afraid that either we are going to be led into a premeditated war or, on the other hand, we shall find ourselves deserted by an isolationist neighbour. That would not be good.
I think the minister and the government ought to feel that the people of this country are behind them in every single thing they do within this third area to keep us out of war, but at the same time to see that aggressors shall not menace any of the peoples in the NATO countries.

One closing suggestion: I have often wondered why we shelved the Atlantic charter. What has happened? We never hear of it any more. But I am going to tell you this, that we have become accustomed to fighting against something a whole lot harder than to fighting for something. And that is a dangerous attitude to get into.
Why should not the western nations adopt and proclaim a charter of freedom-call it the Atlantic charter or any kind of charter you like-a new charter, describing in detail what it stands for? Let us show our good faith by applying it within our own countries -all of us in the NATO organization. To my mind, one good demonstration is worth a million declarations. Give our people the kind of democracy they can believe in and that they are willing to fight for, just as hard as the communist is willing to work and fight for communism. Do that, and we shall not have to worry much longer about the spread of communism.

Mr. Speaker, no matter in what direction one casts his eyes these days, he can see a war going on, or a war about to start, or trouble of other kinds. I feel our government is taking a very proper view in that we are concentrating on the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
I feel that if we are to stay out of trouble, since our affairs are so closely bound up with the old country and with the western European nations, it is absolutely essential that we be strong in this particular field.
There are some which are personal to me and personal to a lot of members of this house. We sent many of our friends and relations to fight in two wars in Europe and we did not see them come back. A lot of us saw fighting at close range and we would not like to get into another war. I for one take a good deal more than academic interest in these matters. I have also had the honour to represent Canada at the United Nations assembly and have seen what efforts are being made to make war impossible. After a lengthy period of development I feel that the United Nations can do a lot toward making the world a real community. However, there are still many reasons why people in America and western Europe should band themselves into a group such as the North Atlantic treaty group. I think they have every right, morally and legally, to do this in spite of what some people in the United Nations have said against NATO.
Every type of federation is divided into states, provinces or other types of groups. In the United Nations we have the Middle East group, the Latin-American- group, the Soviet group and others. I feel we will

make ourselves felt to a much greater degree within the United Nations if we have a strong North Atlantic group.
Referring to our own affairs in this country, we would like to have the luxury of being free of these international obligations. I think everybody agrees with that. We would like to be free to develop our own country. With the technological skills that we have today we can produce in abundance everything that the people of this country could possibly want and we can supply many things to many nations of the world. Our natural resources are second to none. We are an industrious people and I do not think there is a country where the man-day produces as much as it does in Canada. Our banking arrangements through our central bank are such that it would be practically impossible to return to the economic difficulties experienced in the thirties.
As a young nation we should be free to develop the possibilities which stand out before us like a shining light. The United States had a free hand to develop her resources when she was growing because Great Britain and other countries were there to take the brunt of dealing with world affairs. I see no reason why we should not have that same freedom. We should be able to construct the public works which we have on the shelf. We should be able to carry out such projects as the South Saskatchewan river development which would produce revenue. We should be able to do these things as fast as we can.
This government has been accused of making decisions with political advantage in mind. In what better way could that be accomplished than to reduce taxes drastically, build all the public works we want, institute all the public services we feel are desirable and carry out many other projects? We could take full advantage of our bountiful resources. By doing that the government could really make political capital if that is what they had in view.
What is this government doing? It is carrying out things which require sacrifices. It is leaving itself open to criticism such as we hear every day. Why? Because it is taking seriously its international responsibility. It feels that its paramount obligation is to take the steps that are necessary to protect peace and security.
It may be that the Soviet union does not want war any more than we do. Hitler did not want war, but he wanted things which he had no right to want. He wanted nazi control of Europe. He wanted a ring of satellite states around Germany. He wanted Germany to have a place in the sun. But
External Affairs
the time came when decent thinking people could no longer hold up their heads and permit the achievement of Hitler's ambitions.
The western world thought that the British navy and the Maginot line were sufficient protection, but the blitzkrieg and the luftwaffe went over and around the navy and the Maginot line in a matter of hours and days until Great Britain stood with physical equipment not much greater than the oratory of Winston Churchill against bombs and armour. Thank God that Winston Churchill was given the moral power to sustain the free world at that time.
My short incursion into international affairs certainly does not equip me to render fundamental judgments, but I can see and hear and I am able to apply a certain amount of common sense and judgment to what I see and hear. We appear again to be faced with an aggressive nation which is suspicious of the consequences of our reaction to its aggression to the point that a string of oppressed buffer states are felt to be necessary for security. We have Czechoslovakia, Poland, and the other satellite countries.
The ideals which were enunciated at San Francisco are disregarded. Capital is made out of the differences between nations, between classes, between the Asiatic and western races. Over 200 divisions are ready to take the field and a tactical air force of high efficiency is ready to support those divisions. But the decent thinking people of the world have made another decision- they are going to get collectively strong enough to stop this. Responsible people on this side of the Atlantic and in Europe have determined that next time we will not have to rely on the British navy, the Maginot line and the inspiration of a Churchill.
The decisions that these people are making are proving expensive. It seems a pity that we have to put into NATO all the energy and national income that is required to make us strong enough to be able to talk from a position of strength. I think if we can keep our internal thinking straight, if we can get ourselves into a position where no one will think he can gobble us up, we will be able to talk with authority and eventually settle these international issues which perplex and frighten us today. If we are in that position, in my judgment it is almost certain that we can stop this irresponsible show of power and still avert war. That is our only purpose in gathering our strength.
If every shade of thinking in this country were as non-political about these things as this government we could pull through the present situation and come out with flying colours. I am sure that any government

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson), who is a very good friend of mine, it was my privilege to attend the sixth session of the general assembly of the United Nations. Being an adviser of the opposition perhaps I was able to take a slightly more detached point of view than the hon. member for Kindersley. Though I share a great many of the opinions he has expressed, I have never been able to share his enthusiasm for the present administration. However, I do want to take this opportunity to express my thanks to the official members of the Canadian delegation from the minister down to the junior stenographer for the kindly assistance they gave me. No obstacles whatever were placed in my way. I was free to attend any committee I chose. I was granted the privilege of entering into many of the discussions the delegation carried on, and I do feel indebted to all the members of the Canadian delegation without whose help I could not possibly have obtained as much information as I think I did obtain during my attendance at that general assembly.
I would like to give some of my impressions and some of the conclusions I drew from my visit to Paris last fall. I think the first thing that struck me concerning the United Nations was the fact that while many countries were represented, the representation was by no means universal. Reference has been made to that fact already in this debate. Many important countries still are not represented in the United Nations. While 1 share the view already expressed this afternoon that no country which is at least associated with an enemy of the United Nations should be admitted to this family of nations while aggression is still going on, I express the hope that in future it will be possible to embrace more nations of the world and have perhaps a fairer representation of those vast numbers of people who today are not represented at that assembly. But, I repeat, we cannot consider that until such time as aggression has ceased.
The next thing which struck me was the high percentage of the member nations coming from Asia, Africa and areas which might be generally termed, without any disparagement to the individuals concerned, the place of coloured people. The thing which impressed me tremendously was the ability of the delegates from these countries. I could never have believed before I went to Paris that a gentleman 'hailing from Mexico could have maintained discipline in that gathering of many hundreds of delegates in the way that the president of the general assembly did in this last session, and Mr. Nervo came from Mexico.
External Affairs
The third point which struck me was the division of many of these member nations into blocs. I feel that that is regrettable. You had the South American bloc, the Asian bloc and the African people. You had also the Soviet bloc. You had the NATO bloc, if I might call it that, and you had also the British commonwealth bloc. One of the unique things about that group was that quite frequently the various countries agreed to differ on special points, yet at the same time the closest friendship existed.
The fourth point concerned the equality of voting. There was one vote for each representative nation. There again, one has to pause and wonder because there is that bloc to which I have just referred, the Asian and African countries, Abyssinia, Afghanistan and Dominica-all these small countries have the same voting power as the larger countries have.
Then we come to the question of the debates as they were carried out in the general assembly. One could not help feeling that there was a bitterness engendered in many of these debates which were referred to as polemics by Mr. Anthony Eden. I cannot help but think that representatives from countries who go there and indulge in these tactics will soon lose the confidence of the people who have sent them there.
Lastly, there was the question of the proposal for the progressive limitation of arms. It was discussed at considerable length both in the plenary session and in the meetings at the ad hoc and No. 1 committees. I feel that in this case they were doomed to failure before they started because of the unfortunate timing of the NATO meeting in Rome. It gave opportunities for those countries who had suspicions to point to the fact that in Paris certain delegations were talking of the limitation of arms and peace, while a few days later representatives from those same countries went to Rome and talked about rearmament. I repeat that I feel it was unfortunate that those two conferences were arranged to coincide.
I wish to devote a few minutes to discussing the relationship which exists between the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the United Nations itself. We find 'that the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has the appearance of being partly within and partly without the United Nations Organization. For instance, there are certain countries which are not members of the United Nations but are members of NATO. I refer particularly to Italy, for example, and Portugal. Neither of those countries is a member of the United Nations, although both are members of NATO. Then, in a slightly different category you have west Germany, which is not actually

External Affairs
a member of NATO but is becoming closely-associated with that organization, although she is not a member of the United Nations. Spain is coming closely into that orbit. Within the last few days we have read about the United States of America securing bases in Spain for their air operations. No matter how strategically sound that may be, I think it is politically dangerous so long as Spain is not a member of either NATO or the United Nations. I should like the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), if he can, to say whether those bases were obtained for the United States or for the NATO organization. There might be a difference between those two.
The first article of the United Nations charter tells us that the objective of the United Nations is to maintain peace and security, and to that end to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace, and for the suppression of acts of aggression. When the United Nations was first organized immediately after the second world war the objective of the United Nations was not only to endeavour to maintain peace, but to take collective action for the suppression of acts of aggression. Essentially, therefore, the United Nations, in its first conception, was an attempt to deal with the aggressor. We had a rather rude awakening when operations started in Korea, and the United Nations immediately branded the North Koreans as aggressors.
But there was an obvious weakness in the general charter of the United Nations, in that it was only possible to brand North Korea as an aggressor beoause by fortuitous circumstances Russia was not able to exercise her veto. Quite obviously if one of the great powers who, as far back as 1944, were expected always to work in unison-experience has shown that is not practical-were to side with an aggressor, then the United Nations would not be able to designate that country which had committed the act of aggression unless there was some other means than those which existed when operations in Korea broke out.
The second weakness which became so evident was that the United Nations had no force immediately available to suppress that aggression. It was fortunate that the forces of the United States of America were stationed in that area of the world and had been given certain responsibilities for the administration of South Korea. They put in such forces as they had immediately available while the other member nations of the United Nations Organization assembled1 and made such contributions as they were able to make.
[Mr. Pearkes.)
However, the result of the first few months of fighting in Korea was such a close thing that it was not possible to allow similar circumstances to happen again in the future. The United States forces fought rearguard actions down the peninsula of Korea and were at one time threatened with being thrown into the sea and with perhaps the possibility of a "Dunkirk" occurring there. It was too close a thing for the peace-loving people of this world to permit similar circumstances to happen again.
Thought was therefore given as to how these weaknesses could be circumvented. Suggestions were made that if a veto was used in the security council, then immediate reference should be made to the general assembly which could be called in short order for a special session. The suggestion was also made a year ago that the member nations of the United Nations should designate certain -units or formations of their national forces to be placed at the disposal of the United Nations so that they could deal immediately with an aggression. I think that Canada took a lead in that respect. I am not sure how far other countries have followed because since those days the North Atlantic Treaty Organization has been developed. While it may be highly desirable that the United Nations should declare their determination to suppress acts of aggression, no matter where those acts of -aggression might be carried out, we must view that principle with a certain degree of realism. The principle of collective security, applicable the world over, is no doubt extremely desirable; but we cannot allow ourselves to dissipate the limited forces which, in the first instance, would be available to the United Nations, in order to deal with aggression which might break out in some out of the way part of the world. Every hon. member can think of places where an act of aggression- might be committed and where it would be strategically unsound to make large commitments in order to suppress that act of aggression in that particular part of the world. However, if we want to have world opinion behind the United Nations, it is desirable that we endeavour to adhere just as far as it is possible for us to do so, to* this principle of suppressing aggression wherever it may occur.
When the outbreak in Korea took place, we in the west were facing a situation in which our countries had been disarmed to a large extent. Our forces had dissolved immediately after world war II. The traditional policy of Great Britain and other countries has always been to reduce the armed forces, even below

a state of reasonable preparedness to guarantee the security of the country, as soon as peace has been declared. That historic policy was followed out after world war II. On the other hand, however, we found that the Soviet dictatorship maintained huge forces and in their countries worked tirelessly in order to equip those forces they still maintained. We therefore found that time appeared to be at a premium. For that reason I think this North Atlantic treaty was drawn up, in order to meet a possible immediate threat in western Europe.
Had war broken out then, or if war broke out in the immediate future, it would appear that the supreme headquarters of the allied powers in Europe-usually referred to as SHAPE

acting under the instructions of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, would undertake the direction of the operations that they carried out in Europe. Just how the machinery of the United Nations would be employed has not been clearly defined; but it would seem to me that that machinery would have to work in order to obtain the co-operation of members, if any, who were not actually taking part in the operation or were not participating in the various operations.
It is worth while inquiring how we could influence those countries which, in the first place, not being members of NATO, could be influenced to join, to participate and at least to give their moral support. In order to achieve this end, I personally feel that it would be highly desirable if the United Nations could declare the enemy country as the aggressor before any action was taken by the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I realize that there might be serious military objections to a delay which might take place; but those military objections would have to be weighed in the balance in order to see whether the assembling of world opinion on the side of the NATO nations might not compensate for the inevitable delay which would be almost certain to occur had we to wait until the United Nations could designate the enemy as an aggressor. I do stress the fact that it is extremely desirable that we should have world opinion behind us if we are to get the other member countries of the United Nations on our side.
I have referred earlier to these various blocs of countries. I referred to the Asian and African blocs of countries. I had also called attention to the fact that each of these countries has a fighting power equal to the fighting power of any other member country. That great bloc of countries, not closely welded together as yet, but ever growing in importance, is not at the present moment
External Affairs
prepared to accept the philosophy of communism as applied in Russia as being the most desirable form of government or economy for their own countries. Nor are they prepared to accept the western or the American way of life as being that which is most desirable for the future development of their own lands. And so you may say, if you like, they are sitting on the fence, they are undecided and uncertain; that they are not in the position which was held by England in the past, where they are rapidly going to exercise the balance of power between the Soviet bloc and the NATO organization.
If the trend of events develops along that way and we see this large bloc of Asian and African countries waiting to decide which system of ideology they should support, and particularly in a case where perhaps the aggressor has not been named, then I see how very important it is that we should do everything in our power to gain the good will of that bloc of people. At the present moment they are uncertain which way to look. There has been a lot of propaganda coming from Russia, stirring up bitter racial hatred against the so-called colonial powers. There is little recognition of the fact that the so-called colonial powers had raised those countries out of slavery. On the other hand, there is too much talk of the fact that they have taken our natural resources and sold the manufactured goods to us at great profit.
However, we must remember that there is that feeling of nationalism, which the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) referred to, growing up amongst these countries. It is particularly evident in the Arab countries. There is difficulty amongst these Arab countries of the Middle East. For five hundred years they had been under the domination of Turkey. Turkey has now become a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I do not think it is going to make these Arab countries one bit more friendly to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. They are suspicious of Britain; they are suspicious of America. At the present time thousands of them are almost on the verge of starvation in countries surrounding Israel. But I do regard this bloc of Asian and African countries as being a tremendous influence in the immediate future.
Possibly India is the leader of that group. The last half of this century may be India's. I feel that the opportunity which is offered to Canada and to Great Britain of influencing that bloc through our associations in the commonwealth with India is tremendous.

External Affairs
Therefore I feel that, in discussing this question of the relative position of NATO and the United Nations, we must stress the fact that NATO is complementary to and in no way competitive with the United Nations. I am not certain that that viewpoint is held by all. There is the possibility, rightly or wrongly, that NATO will be viewed as a rival of the United Nations Organization. I hold in my hand a heading from the Montreal Star of March 5 as follows: "NATO now replaces UN, says Pearson." I give the Secretary of State for External Affairs the benefit by stating at once that the text of the report would not justify, in my opinion, such a heading being given.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It would not.

But, at the same time, it is indicative of a feeling which perhaps exists and a feeling which may exist amongst those other countries that are not members of NATO. That will apply not only to the military commitments, but also to clause 2, which deals with the economic side, because many of these countries that I have been referring to are underdeveloped, backward countries, and are jealous of seeing any money which they think should come their way being sent in another direction.
I have referred to the organization of the allied command, SHAPE, which exists with headquarters just outside of Paris. That organization consists of three main parts, the allied forces of northern Europe, the allied forces of central Europe, and the allied forces of southern Europe. The grouping of these nations which are forming part of NATO, or the forces of these nations, into these three, may I call them commands, needs no more elaboration. In the north, naturally, you have the forces of Norway and Denmark; in the south, until recently, you had the forces of Italy and Portugal. I presume that the forces of Greece and of Turkey will be added to that southern European command. What I would like to ask the minister is to what extent are the Canadian forces-because I do not think we should ask him for information about other forces- committed to the allied forces, central Europe? Would it be possible for the commander-in-chief of the supreme headquarters to transfer these forces, we will say, to Norway or to Italy, to the northern or southern command without a reference to the council of NATO? That is a question which I hope he will be able to explain at a later date, because I do feel that it has a very definite bearing upon our commitment. The people of Canada should know whether the commander in chief has full authority to

transfer our forces from, shall I say, one theatre of operation to another without reference to the political authority which is supreme over the military forces.
In the terms in which that has been put, he has no such authority.
I did not hear the minister.
In the terms in which I understand the hon. member has put it, he has no such authority.
That is the information that I wanted to have.
On the other hand, we regard his recommendation.
Naturally, his recommendation would carry weight. But he would have to go to toe council of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, on which we have a responsible minister representing the country.
And the Canadian government would make the decision, in the end. But on the other hand, we will co-operate.

That is the information I wanted to obtain. I should like to close my remarks with one word of warning, if it might be considered as such, with respect to the employment of our own forces which are in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
I do not suppose there is any sphere of human activity in which the lessons of history are more worthy of study than in that of military operations. It is common knowledge that the influence of Britain in wars in the past has always been most effective when small, yet highly trained forces have taken advantage of Britain's command of the seas. The result has been that these forces have influenced; operations to an extent out of all proportion to their size.
In world1 war I the armies of the commonwealth bogged down in the mud of Flanders and there, for several years, we suffered heavy casualties. Dunkirk saved the armies of world war II from another war of attrition. Bearing in mind those lessons, I do suggest that any excessive or premature commitment of Canadian troops, and particularly air force, to the continent of Europe, may find us once again shackled to continental and land-bound operations.
The principles that applied to the army and navy in the past apply with added force to the air force of today, the service which has as its greatest attribute its flexibility and its ability to strike in unexpected places. If the surrender of freedom of action of the R.C.A.F. is the price we must pay to increase

European morale, then I say it is indeed' a high price. Therefore I urge that periodically the policy of dispatching our jet fighter squadrons to Europe be reviewed in order to see that we consider fully the principle of retaining our flexibility to manoeuvre and the ability to send our squadrons where they are most required as well as the retention in Canada of sufficient squadrons to defend effectively the many important industrial targets of this country, the loss of which would be not only a crippling blow to the NATO organization, but also fatal to Canada.
I know that, according to the plans, there are these twelve jet squadrons which ultimately will be sent to Europe. I do suggest that that should be contingent upon the development and progress made in the squadrons which are required primarily for the defence of Canada. We should not send over to Europe the first twelve squadrons we get, and leave Canada unprotected. There should also be review time and again with regard to
External Affairs
the necessity for having such a high percentage of our very mobile air forces tied down to airfields in France, airfields which at the present time have not been constructed or are not available, and which France up to now has shown some reluctance to make available-and which under any circumstances could only be regarded as being highly vulnerable, owing to the disturbed conditions which exist, particularly in France, but also on the continent as a whole.
I offer that suggestion in the light of historical experience which time and time again has emphasized the importance of utilizing the manoeuvrability that in bygone days was provided by the command of the seas by the British navy, and is today available to the air forces of this country.
